newsitem.title: USA: Harcourt makes rival bid for National Education.
newsitem.headline: Harcourt makes rival bid for National Education.

text.p: Publisher Harcourt General Inc. Wednesday launched a $740 million cash takeover bid for National Education Corp., topping the stock deal struck last month between the training services company and Sylvan Learning Systems Inc.
Harcourt, based in Chestnut Hill, Mass., said its $19.50 per share tender offer followed an intensive review of National Education.

Harcourt has "concluded that the strategic and financial advantages of combining our two companies are too compelling to ignore," Harcourt Chairman Richard Smith wrote in a letter to National Education Chief Executive Officer Sam Yau.

An acquisition of National Education would extend the reach of Harcourt, known best as a traditional textbook publisher, into the growing areas of supplemental educational materials and correspondence courses.
"These are markets we have had an interest in. They fit very well into the company," said Harcourt spokesman Peter Farwell.
National Education could not be reached for comment.
But Columbia, Md.-based Sylvan said it would proceed with its planned transaction.

"The benefits of combining Sylvan and NEC have been evidenced to us for some time and the offer by Harcourt General validates our view of the inherent value of NEC. We continue to view the combination of Sylvan and NEC as the best way to create value for the shareholders of both companies and we are proceeding as planned to finalise the transaction," Sylvan President Doug Becker said in a statement.
Wall Street analysts said the Harcourt General bid was likely to entice shareholders who are nervous about the company's volatile month-old transaction with Sylvan.
"We believe this Harcourt offer is attractive to shareholders and is superior to Sylvan's," wrote Raymond James & Associates Inc. analyst John Mayhoney in a report to clients.
The Harcourt bid comes as the value of National Education's planned deal with Sylvan has eroded in recent weeks due to a decline in Sylvan's stock.

Originally worth $750 million, the value of the National Education-Sylvan transaction had eroded to $625 million earlier this week. Under the plan with Sylvan, shareholders of National Education would receive 0.58 share of Sylvan for each share held.
Sylvan shares rose after Harcourt announced its bid, raising the value of the proposed transaction to $647 million -- still less than Harcourt General's cash offer.
Based in Irvine, Calif., National Education provides educational training services, including supplemental textbooks and correspondence courses.
Analysts said Harcourt, which is sitting on a cash stockpile of about $800 million, could raise its $19.50 offer if Sylvan tries to compete.

They also said Sylvan would be hardpressed to offer cash in the deal and would likely only sweeten the exchange ratio in its existing transaction -- a move that could dilute earnings and further pressure Sylvan's share price.

"I think it's very good for the shareholders and the management of NEC. I would take Harcourt if I were the shareholders. In the long run, Harcourt can really win it hands down," said Ivan Obolensky of New York investment firm Shields & Co.

National Education stock soared $4.375 to $19.375 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Sylvan shares gained $1 to $30.125 on Nasdaq and Harcourt rose $2.125 to $45 per share on the NYSE.
Harcourt also said in the letter that it would prefer to negotiate a friendly transaction, but took the offer directly to National "to underscore the seriousness of our intentions."

Harcourt said that if its plan to acquire National Education succeeds, it will seek to acquire the outstanding shares of Steck Vaughn Publishing Corp. not already owned by National Education, at $14 per share.
Steck shares rose $2.50 to $13 on Nasdaq.
Harcourt also disclosed that it had expressed interest in National Education in 1994, but a transaction was never reached.
